title: What is science? Even scientists can't agree
gist: A Royal Society Open Science study (Dubova and Liu; 91 scientists, 99 public, 18 descriptions of science) finds scientists disagree more than the public about what science is, even within subfields, while the public holds an idealized truth-machine view; the gap may fuel frustration when findings are revised, and Dubova warns AI-automated discovery could lock in one narrow conception of science.

themes.theme: Scientists disagree on what science is

insights.claim: A study in Royal Society Open Science surveying 91 scientists and 99 members of the public on 18 historical descriptions of science found scientists disagree about science's meaning and purpose more than the general public does.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Expert consensus on methodology is weaker than assumed; treat 'the science says' claims as contingent on which research philosophy produced them.
insights.quote: scientists disagree about the meaning and purpose of science even more than the general public does

insights.claim: Of 18 descriptions of science tested, few received unqualified endorsement from scientists, and disagreement existed even among scientists within the same subfield.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Intra-field methodological divergence means research outputs from the same discipline may not be comparable; diligence the lab's approach, not just the field.
insights.quote: there was quite a bit of disagreement between scientists, including scientists who are in the same subfield

insights.claim: Scientists broadly agree only that science involves curiosity-driven exploration and solving mysteries; they split on whether it is a search for objective truth versus driven by human judgment and creativity, and on whether research follows established methods or requires improvisation.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: The truth-seeking vs. creative-judgment split is a useful lens for evaluating research organizations and R&D cultures.

insights.claim: Dubova suspects scientists' divergent conceptions of science arise because they develop their own approaches through experience, like chefs who disagree about cooking.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Tacit, experience-built methodology is hard to standardize or transfer, which matters for scaling R&D teams and codifying research into automated systems.

themes.theme: Public's idealized view and trust friction

insights.claim: The general public holds a more uniform, idealized view of science as a reliable process for uncovering objective truths, with less emphasis on creativity or uncertainty than scientists place.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: The expectation gap between public and practitioners is a structural source of trust erosion when findings are revised.
insights.quote: a more uniform and idealized view of science as a reliable process for uncovering objective truths

insights.claim: The gap between public and scientific views of science may explain why people become frustrated when scientists cannot give definitive answers or revise conclusions as new evidence emerges, and may shape which discoveries scientists pursue and how the public judges them.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Watch for policy and funding backlash in areas where evidence evolves quickly (e.g., public health); communication of uncertainty is a reputational risk factor.

insights.claim: The public's views of science align more closely with physicists and biologists than with psychologists or social scientists, possibly because physics and biology are more prominent in science education, though the link is unconfirmed.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: Social-science findings face a steeper public legitimacy hurdle, relevant when such research informs policy or markets.
insights.locator: Interestingly, the public's views were closer

insights.claim: Dubova worries that AI systems built to conduct scientific research could, by automating discovery, entrench one narrow understanding of science at the expense of other valuable approaches.
insights.speaker: @sfiscience
insights.so_what: AI-for-science platforms embed a methodological philosophy; diversity of approaches may be a differentiator and monoculture a hidden risk for the AI research-automation trend.
insights.quote: automating discovery could reinforce one narrow understanding of science at the expense of other valuable approaches
